item.title: Stages of Compilation
item.description: Before jumping straight to compiler optimizations, which is what most of this chapter is about, let’s briefly recap the “big picture” first. Skipping the boring parts, there are 4 stages of turning C programs into executables: Preprocessing expands macros, pulls included source from header files, and removes comments: gcc -E source.c (writes preprocessed source to standard output). Compilation parses the source, diagnoses errors, converts it into intermediate representations, performs optimizations, and emits assembly: gcc -S source.

item.title: Flags and Targets
item.description: The first step of getting high performance from the compiler is to ask for it, which is done with over a hundred different compiler options, attributes, and pragmas. #Optimization LevelsThere are 4 and a half main levels of optimization for speed in GCC: -O0 is the default one that does no optimizations (although, in a sense, it does optimize: for compilation time). -O1 (also aliased as -O) does a few “low-hanging fruit” optimizations, almost not affecting the compilation time.

item.title: Situational Optimizations
item.description: The optimizations enabled by -O2 and -O3 are selected because they are broadly profitable, not because they are guaranteed to improve every program. Transformations can increase code size, disturb layout, or optimize for a workload unlike yours. Options outside -O3 are often non-standard-compliant or especially situational and require more information from the programmer. Let’s discuss the most frequently used ones that we’ve also previously covered in this book. #Loop UnrollingCompilers already unroll some small loops when their trip count and profitability are clear.

item.title: Contract Programming
item.description: Memory-safe language subsets such as safe Rust sharply restrict the operations that can cause undefined behavior. They can still report errors, panic, run out of resources, or leave details such as hash-table iteration order to an implementation; “safe” does not mean that every operation succeeds. C and C++ expose a larger set of operations with undefined behavior. If a program evaluates one of them, the language places no requirements on the result.

item.title: Non-Zero-Cost Abstractions
item.description: Consider two perfectly reasonable ways of storing a matrix: std::vector<std::vector<float>> a(n, std::vector<float>(m)); std::vector<float> b(n * m); Both let us address an element using two indices. Both take $O(nm)$ space. Both can be hidden behind an interface called Matrix. But only one is actually a matrix in memory. The first representation contains $n$ separately allocated vectors. Reading a[i][j] first loads the pointer to row $i$ and only then loads the element. Rows are not guaranteed to be adjacent, and constructing or destroying the matrix performs $n+1$ allocations.

item.title: Precomputation
item.description: When a compiler can prove that a value does not depend on runtime input, it may calculate the value during compilation and embed the result into the program. This optimization is called constant folding. Constant folding is permitted by the C++ as-if rule, but it is not guaranteed merely because all arguments happen to be literals. A compiler may decide that a computation is too expensive to perform while compiling, or may simply miss the opportunity.

item.title: Arithmetic Optimizations
item.description: Here is a function that divides an unsigned integer by ten: #include <cstdint> std::uint32_t div10(std::uint32_t x) { return x / 10; } There is no reason for this tiny function to be interesting, except that its machine code normally contains no division. Optimizing compilers replace the constant divisor with a multiplication by a precomputed reciprocal followed by a shift. The derivation is subtle enough to occupy a good part of the integer division chapter, yet the optimization happens without being requested.

item.title: What Compilers Can and Can't Do
item.description: Suppose a program spends most of its time looking up strings in a sorted vector. Replacing the vector with a hash table would make the workload faster. Why does -O3 not do it for us? Because this is not an optimization in the compiler sense. A hash table uses more memory, iterates in a different order, invalidates references under different conditions, has different worst-case behavior, and requires a hash function whose cost and security properties depend on the application.
